source.title: Training Trajectories of Language Models Across Scales
source.authors: Mengzhou Xia; Mikel Artetxe; Chunting Zhou; Xi Victoria Lin; Ramakanth Pasunuru; Danqi Chen; Luke Zettlemoyer; Ves Stoyanov

record.tranche_reason: The study reports validation-perplexity trajectories with double-descent-like behavior for selected token subsets, but also finds that the aggregate validation perplexity declines and that the pattern depends on which tokens are selected. This refines the scope of epoch-wise double descent rather than reproducing the original interpolation-threshold experiments.
record.gate_note: The direct result relevant to the claim is token-level validation perplexity over training checkpoints (Figure 4 and related text). The paper does not test data-set sample-size changes, locate an interpolation threshold, or test label noise or regularization dependence. Its model-size scaling and sequence-generation results do not establish a model-wise double-descent curve near an interpolation threshold.
record.test_reason: The study tracks held-out per-token perplexity across OPT pre-training checkpoints (125M–175B). It reports a fall-rise-fall ('double descent-like') trajectory over training on certain token subsets, while aggregate validation perplexity falls throughout. This bears on V2 in a new setting: LM pre-training, plotted against FLOPs, about 1.7 passes over the data. It is better classed T3 than T5 because the authors do not argue V2 is wrong; they report it appearing in a new setting. No result locates an interpolation threshold, varies sample size, or varies noise or regularization.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also interpret the pattern as larger models first overfitting a token subset and then generalizing on it. They say it occurs consistently across scales and at similar validation perplexity. They offer no explanation and do not know whether it is an artifact of the data, the objective or the optimization.
record.recipe_differences: Studies intermediate OPT language-model checkpoints and validation perplexity trajectories for token subsets; it does not reproduce the original model-size, epoch, or sample-size interpolation-threshold experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported trajectory depends on the selected token subset and on which model and training percentage are used to select it.

fits_no_version.finding: Texts decoded with the ps−pl configuration show inverse scaling: perplexity rises with model size. On these texts, 125M checkpoints trend downward over training while 1.3B and larger go down, then up.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-monotone scaling and training trajectories of model perplexity on small-model-favoured text, which is distinct from interpolation-threshold double descent.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The direct double-descent evidence is for selected token subsets, not aggregate test error. The authors state that their criteria capture only around 60% of tokens, and that trajectories of uncategorized tokens are inconsistent across models. They also say they do not explain the cause of the behavior.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows left out; the included rows cover the aggregate validation-perplexity trajectories and the main token-subset trajectories described in Figure 4 and §3.2.

untested.parts: No label-noise or regularization variation and no link to an interpolation threshold. The x-axis is training FLOPs over about 1.7 data passes, not multiple epochs. There is no aggregate test-error double descent; only selected token subsets show it.
No model-size sweep against an interpolation threshold.
No effective-complexity measure. Validation-perplexity alignment across sizes (Fig. 12) is suggestive but is not tested as a predictor of the peak's location.
No noise or regularization manipulation and no test for multiple peaks.

missing.what: Tokens selected by 6.7B (and by 13B and 30B) after 10% or 40% of training. Larger models rise, and only 175B shows a second descent; at 40% the change is milder.

Uncategorized tokens (about 40% of all tokens). After 10% of training, 125M, 1.3B and 6.7B show a slight double descent and larger models show downward or stagnated trends. After 40%, only 125M shows a slight double descent.
The same upward-trend trajectories plotted against validation perplexity. Models larger than 1.3B overlap on a double-descent-like curve.

record.verdict_notes: Measures and setting: held-out next-token perplexity on PG-19 validation lines (about 102K context-token pairs). OPT is trained on 300B tokens, 180B of them unique. Checkpoints are sparse (18–36 per model) and plotted against FLOPs, not epochs. Trend categories come from per-token regression significance, so tokens are selected on noisy series and regression to the mean may affect cross-model curves. The paper gives no numeric peak heights.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep locating a peak near the size that just fits the training set. The paper reports other scaling results, but does not test this version's interpolation-threshold claim.
Measures validation perplexity, including selected subsets of context-token pairs, rather than aggregate classification test error; does not report curves against epochs specifically.
No sweep over the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold.
No comparison across model classes testing general double descent.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated across size, training time, and sample size.
Does not test whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether regularization removes it, or whether multiple peaks occur.
Does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters.
